idiom_name: private field + checked methods; class delegation (by) for transparent guards; Delegates.vetoable for refused writes
implementation_notes: Kotlin's visibility is compiler-enforced within the build unit: a member marked private 'is visible inside this class only', internal means 'any client inside this module who sees the declaring class sees its internal members', and a module is 'a set of Kotlin files compiled together' - a build-unit boundary rather than a security boundary (the test source set can reach internal declarations). The guard is therefore a class with a private resource field and public methods that check the policy first; where the guard must keep the resource's own interface, class delegation makes the compiler generate the forwarding ('A class Derived can implement an interface Base by delegating all of its public members to a specified object'), and the guard overrides exactly the operations it must check. Delegated properties add a per-access hook for the write side: Delegates.vetoable invokes its handler before the assignment, so a guard can refuse a change instead of forwarding it. The documented leak is interop - 'internal declarations become public in Java' (only the names are mangled) - so the class/process boundary, not the modifier alone, has to carry the security claim.
pitfalls: internal is not private: 'internal declarations become public in Java', so any JVM language can call them (only the mangled name stands in the way) - keep the resource private when the guard must hold.

Class delegation forwards every public member of the delegate that you do not override: the guard's surface equals the delegate's surface, so override or avoid anything privileged instead of assuming `by` narrows it.

Delegated properties route every access through getValue/setValue and store the delegate in a hidden field; a custom delegate must check inside those operators, and Delegates.vetoable guards only writes through that property, not the backing object's own API.
JVM reflection can still reach what Kotlin's compiler hides, so treat private/internal as design boundaries; process isolation is what resists code that runs with the same privileges.
